stories.title: It’s unfashionable to say it, but class still matters – and young people know that | Polly Toynbee
stories.description: From inheritance to nepotism in the workplace, social inequality is now a daily experience for many young people This should come as no great surprise: young people are more keenly aware of the significance of social class than those who came before them. The yawning gap in life chances at birth is something they know better than complacent older generations. Class may be unfashionable in the language of politics – long damned by the right as the politics of envy, avoided by many on the left for fear of sounding chip-on-the-shoulder – yet it’s part of the daily experience for young people. Nearly half of 16- to 34-year-olds in the UK now say class is important to their identity – and not in a good way – according to a new Ipsos poll . That’s nearly twice as many as among the over-55s. Maybe that’s because more young people are better educated at each level, so they know more, with a grounding in reasoned thinking. stories.description: I welcome Alan Milburn’s call for schools to focus more on students’ potential beyond exams. Yet I must ask: where is the money? At 16, life should feel like a path leading to endless opportunities. That is at least the carrot dangled in front of young people to motivate them through the gruelling years of exam preparation. “Your life starts now,” their teachers all but tell them. And though for the vast majority that is true, there is a cohort who are forced to accept that the bright futures they were promised are beyond their reach. They are the nearly one million young people aged between 16 and 24 who are not in education, employment or training (Neets). stories.description: Amazon Ring has finally announced their long-dreaded indoor drone , a small flying surveillance device connected to their security suite of products that can fly around your house filming and recording things. The device is supposedly designed to fly preset paths across your home and will also activate if a sensor or alarm has been triggered. Customers should think twice about purchasing these devices for a number of reasons. These devices are problematic in many of the ways we’ve said Ring’s stationary home surveillance products are a problem , plus some new ways. At a very basic level, they are essentially a window into your house that can be accessed by anyone with access to your account—which has historically included bad actors looking to embarrass or harass Ring users and employees of the company .
